items.definition: Introduces a statement that contrasts with what was said before. It usually starts a new sentence and is followed by a comma.
examples: The hotel was cheap. However, the rooms were very small.
The route is longer; however, it is much more scenic.

items.definition: Introduces a clause that contrasts with the main clause. Do not use but in the same sentence.
examples: Although it was raining, we walked to the station.
I enjoyed the film, although the ending was predictable.

items.definition: Compares two things or people by showing how they are different.
examples: My sister loves city life, whereas I prefer the countryside.
Revenue grew in Spain, whereas it fell in Italy.

items.definition: Introduces a point that is true in spite of what has just been said; stronger and more formal than however.
examples: The results were disappointing. Nevertheless, the team has not given up.
The task is difficult; nevertheless, it can be done.

items.definition: Adds a further point that supports or strengthens the previous one; common in essays and reports.
examples: The scheme is expensive. Moreover, it has not reduced traffic.
The flat is close to work; moreover, the rent is reasonable.

items.definition: Introduces a second, opposite point of view or fact when you are comparing two sides of something.
examples: Living in the centre is convenient. On the other hand, it can be noisy.
Flying is faster; on the other hand, the train is greener.

items.definition: Introduces a result or conclusion that follows logically from the previous statement.
examples: The road is closed; therefore, buses are being diverted.
Sales fell last year. We have therefore decided to cut costs.

items.definition: Shows that what follows happened because of what has just been mentioned.
examples: She trained hard all summer. As a result, she won the regional title.
The shop lost a lot of customers and, as a result, had to close.

items.definition: Adds another reason, often a stronger one, in informal speech. Do not confuse it with beside, which means next to.
examples: I don't fancy going out; besides, I have an early start tomorrow.
It's too expensive, and besides, we don't really need it.

items.definition: Adds a further, often surprising or stronger, point in speech or informal writing.
examples: The hotel was spotless and, what's more, it was cheap.
He passed the test first time. What's more, he got full marks.

items.definition: Adds a comment that slightly weakens or qualifies what you have just said; typical of casual British speech.
examples: The food was awful. Mind you, we did arrive very late.
It's a lovely flat. Mind you, I wouldn't want to climb those stairs daily.

items.definition: Introduces a condition that must be met for the main statement to be true; stronger than if.
examples: You can borrow the car, provided that you bring it back by six.
The scheme will go ahead provided that enough people sign up.

items.definition: Shows that something happened although there was an obstacle. It is followed by a noun or an -ing form, never directly by a clause, and without of.
examples: Despite the heavy traffic, we arrived on time.
He kept working despite feeling ill.
